title: Given a 2D board of characters and a word, return true if the word exists in the grid by connecting horizontally or vertically adjacent cells, where each cell is used at most once.
shortTitle: Word Search: DFS on a grid with visited marking
keyPoints: DFS from each cell matching the first letter, advancing through the word character by character
Mark cells visited by temporarily overwriting with a sentinel; restore on backtrack
The search succeeds when the word index reaches the word length, meaning all characters matched
Short-circuit OR across four directions returns immediately on the first successful path
Worst-case time is O(rows * cols * 4^L) where L is the word length
A letter-frequency pre-check can fail fast when the board lacks enough of any required letter

s1_definition.oneliner: DFS from each matching start, mark cells visited along the path, unmark on backtrack, succeed when the word is fully matched.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Word Search** finds whether a word can be traced in a grid by moving up, down, left, or right, using each cell at most once.
- **DFS with backtracking** tries each direction, marking the current cell to prevent reuse and restoring it on backtrack.
- **Success condition** is when the character index reaches the word length, meaning every character has been matched.
- **Short-circuit OR** across four directions returns true as soon as any path succeeds.
- **Worst-case time** is O(R * C * 4^L); **space** is O(L) for the recursion stack.
s1_definition.analogy: On a stamped grid of characters at the National Bank of India, Rajesh must verify a security phrase by tracing it through adjacent characters without stepping on the same cell twice. He places a finger on a starting character, moves to adjacent matching characters, and if he completes the phrase the grid passes. If he gets stuck, he backtracks and tries another path.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Word Search is grid backtracking. You scan the board for cells matching the first letter and launch a DFS from each, carrying the index of the next character to match. The search succeeds when the index reaches the word length. At each cell you mark it visited by temporarily overwriting its character, try all four directions, and restore the character on backtrack so other paths can reuse it.

The temporary overwrite trick avoids a separate visited array: the sentinel character does not match any letter in the word, so the guard rejects any path that tries to revisit a cell on the current path. The short-circuit OR across directions returns immediately on the first success.

The worst case is O(R * C * 4^L), which is exponential in the word length. In practice, mismatches prune most branches early. A letter-frequency pre-check can fail fast when the board does not have enough of every required letter, and searching the word in reverse when the last character is rarer than the first can improve performance.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh used this to verify security phrases embedded in a stamped character grid. The DFS-with-restore pattern traced the phrase through adjacent cells, and the frequency pre-check quickly rejected grids that lacked required characters.

Remember one sentence: mark with a sentinel before recursing, restore on backtrack, and the search succeeds when every character in the word has been matched.
